ui.title: The Hundred Misdeeds
ui.sub: — The Demon Lord died leaving a hundred misdeeds. Every one of them was a lie. —

chapters: VI. To You Who Read This

t: In the year 471 of the Dark Calendar, Veil, the Shrouded Demon Lord, ravaged the continent with one hundred misdeeds. Villages burned, the great river ran with poison, and three hundred children were stolen away.
Yet from those ashes rose the hero Ash, who bound the swords of the kingdoms into one and, after five years of war, struck the Demon Lord down at last. And so the world was saved—
Everything up to this line is the lie I wrote for the world.

Let me be precise. I did not write a single falsehood. The villages did burn. The river did change color. The children did vanish. I did kill the Demon Lord, and the world truly was saved. Every line of it, fact.
How to lie using nothing but facts—that, I learned from her.

This is the forbidden book that the man called hero, author of the official chronicle, leaves behind in a single copy. If you must burn it, do so after you finish. But be warned: when you close the last page, you will no longer be able to hate that Demon Lord properly.
If you can live with that, turn the page.
There was no treasure in the Demon Lord's castle.

The officials sent to appraise the spoils gave up within three days. Not one gold coin. The armory half empty, and the study larger than the throne room. "Frugal creature, this Demon Lord," someone laughed. I could not laugh.
That the castle of the monster I had killed smelled of nothing but books—somehow, that grated on me.

I returned to this castle half a year after the subjugation. The allied kingdoms had ordered me to compile the official history. The Chronicle of the Demon War, written by the hero himself. No finer textbook, so went the reasoning.

The world outside was mid-festival. In every town square they burned effigies of the Demon Lord while children kicked up the ashes, laughing. Half a year after the war, and people had not stopped hating. Hatred is fun enough to become a festival. I know that better than anyone.
For twelve years, I held that festival in my chest, every single night.
I did not refuse the post, because I wanted material. Material to keep hating.

I will confess: I was hollow. Take the Demon Lord away from a man who has burned her as his only fuel for twelve years, and nothing remains but the cinders. Night after night I touched the name tag at my chest, searching myself for proof I could still hate.

The sole survivor of a burned village, a child of six—that is me. A six-year-old should remember something, yet of that night I have almost nothing. Only fire, and smoke, and the stiffness of a black cloak that carried me as it ran.
When I was found at the temple gate, an old name tag was tied to my collar. The first thing that was ever mine.
So I meant to write out the Demon Lord's crimes, from one to one hundred, every last line.
I still dream of the final battle. The Demon Lord laughing as she coughed blood. The lips that tried to say something as my blade went in. I wrote it down as begging for her life.
At the very back of the study, on a shelf without even a lock, the ledger was waiting.
A black leather spine. The title, handwritten:
A Register of Misdeeds
Inside, meticulous writing in neat rows. A tidy, oddly dutiful hand that slanted upward to the right. Misdeeds One through One Hundred, each with a date, a place, and a count of the dead.
"Misdeed No. 73. Burned the village of Liese. Two hundred fourteen residents, dead."

A Demon Lord who numbered her own crimes in sequence. The final entry, dated—politely—the very morning of our last battle. Madness with perfect penmanship, I thought at the time. Print this in the appendix and she would be hated for a hundred years.
Exactly as she intended.
"Lord Ash. Your tea is ready."
Mia, the healer who had traveled with me since the war, set down the tray. She had volunteered to assist with the compilation herself.
Come to think of it—I remember the thought crossing my mind—in three days in this castle, Mia had not once lost her way. The kitchen, the well; she walked as if she had always known where they were.
At the time, I only thought her quick-witted.
An official history demands evidence. I sent inquiries to every kingdom and began verifying the misdeeds, one entry at a time.
The first to crumble was No. 73.

Liese village, two hundred fourteen dead. And yet, comb the kingdom's registries however I might, not one death certificate had been filed in Liese that year. Lost in the chaos of the burning?—I began to think so, then noticed the opposite. It was not that the certificates were missing.
The names of the two hundred fourteen dead matched no registry at all.

Instead, something strange surfaced. Settlement records in the Demon Lord's territory, five years later. Families of curiously similar composition, under new names—exactly two hundred fourteen people.
And three days before the burning, the Demon Lord had posted a proclamation in the village: "Within three days, this village burns."
Why would a threat bother to name a deadline?

I had every proclamation of the Demon Lord collected. All of them. Every one carried a deadline. Burn you within three days. Cut your water within seven. Those theatrical decrees I had taken for hate-mongering collapse, reread, into a single sentence.
—You have three days. Run.

Only one was an exception. The last proclamation, issued the night before our final battle: "Whosoever touches my land and my people after my death shall bear a curse unto the last generation." This one alone had no deadline. At the time it was mocked as a dying woman's spite. I mocked it too.
If the deadlines were windows to escape, this one page alone refused to be reread.
I traveled to the valley in the settlement records, my identity hidden. A junior clerk to the royal historian, so I claimed.

The fields were small but well tilled. The old farmer I visited was, I am certain, a survivor of Liese. On the handle of an old plow in his barn, a half-scraped name remained—a name that existed only in Liese's registry, and nowhere on any list of the dead.
"Tell me about Liese village," I said.
The old man was silent a long while, then poured two cups of tea. One he passed to me. The other he set before an empty seat.
"...I don't talk about dead villages. Made it a rule."

That was all. As I left, he studied my face from the doorway. He knew, I think. From the moment the children at the valley's mouth ran ahead with the news, the whole valley likely knew. The man who killed the Demon Lord has come.
Even so, no one threw a stone. No one shouted the truth. The old man said just one thing.
"Master Hero. That face of yours ain't getting any better."
How could it. Back then I did not understand even half of what I was digging into. My body understood before I did.
That Liese had been a village infected with the Ashen Haze—I learned it the following week.

The Ashen Haze. These days even its dead are counted among the victims of the Demon Lord's curse. It was I who struck the disease's name from the official history, though perhaps I needn't have bothered. People are far better at counting enemies than at counting diseases. The kingdoms' method, back then, was simple.
Send the army to any infected village. They called it "purification." It meant burning the village, residents included.
A village burned by the Demon Lord was a village the army never had to burn.

Flames over an emptied village were quarantine—and rampart. A village burned by the Demon Lord was declared "defiled ground" and sealed; the army skipped inspection and reported the war result. There is no safer shroud than a ruin no one examines.
No. 41. Poisoned the great river Sol. The famous one—the banks clouded over silver.

I investigated the three cities downstream, hunting for the poison's victims. I found the opposite. That winter, in those three cities alone, the Ashen Haze claimed no one. At the time it was called a miracle—the Hero's Blessing. A miracle that wore my name.
The answer was in an old formulary of the Royal Infirmary. Alvengrass, the specific remedy—a phantom drug so costly it had vanished into war budgets. Its decoction clouds silver.
In the ledger's margins, dense little figures. Flow rate, dilution, days to arrival. The calculations I had long thought odd for a poisoning plan were dosage.
The silver banks can still be visited. I went. At dusk the river's surface still gleams as if brushed with silver. An old fisherman mending his nets on the levee spoke without my asking.
"Cursed river, they hollered. Next year the fish doubled."

For five years I hated it and called it poison. But consider. Hand out the Demon Lord's medicine, and whoever takes it hangs as a collaborator. Pour it in a well, and that village burns. A medicine that could pass every checkpoint, that no one could refuse and no one could be blamed for—only a river. If it had not worn the shape of a curse, it could not have arrived at all.
No. 22. Ten years ago. The abduction of three hundred children.
By the time I came to verify this one, my hands went cold at every turn of the page. Premonitions strike truest precisely when you pray they won't.
The three hundred taken were, all of them, orphans of the Ashen Haze. Parents burned, or abandoned by them—children no place in any kingdom would take.
In the margins of the register, there were names.
"Mira, six. Breaks out in a rash from tree nuts."
"Toto, nine. Cries at night. Do not put out the light."
"Sena, five. Hard of hearing, left ear. Speak from the right."
I held the page and could not move for a while.

Why would a record of crimes need a note about night crying? Why would a ledger of abductions log a nut rash? This is not the record of a crime. This is—a handover. Written by one caretaker of children, for the next.
And there, in that same column, it was.
"Mia, seven. Weak against milk."
In all our travels, she never once touched milk. I knew that. I had watched her beside me for three years.
Mia did not run, and did not hide.
When I pointed to the name, she quietly bowed her head.
"Yes. I was inside the twenty-second misdeed."

Then she told me everything. The orphans raised in the Demon Lord's land. The people of burned villages tilling fields under new names. The eccentric master of the castle kitchen. No wonder she never lost her way. She grew up in this castle.
"You knew? All of it?"
"Everyone from her land does."
"Then why did no one say it? I— we went to kill your benefactor."
Mia shook her head. Her eyes neither accused nor forgave.
"Being hated was how she protected us. So no one corrected it. Correct it, and her twelve years come to nothing."
The children of the Demon Lord's land, she said, are taught exactly one rule.
—Never say thank you to her.

Because gratitude leaks. One "thank you" reaching a traveler's ear would tear a hole in the shroud. So the valley's children grow up rehearsing insults for their benefactor. The Demon Lord is stingy. The Demon Lord is mean. The Demon Lord is heartless.
Saying it over and over, they gather in her kitchen and spoon down the porridge she made.
"Our 'heartless,'" Mia said, "probably reached her better than any 'thank you' in the world."
That night, I learned who the Demon Lord Veil had been.

Theodora Veil. Until twelve years ago, the youngest chief epidemiologist the Royal Infirmary had ever appointed. When she fell from grace she was a girl of sixteen. As the Ashen Haze began to spread she kept urging the kingdoms: quarantine across borders, mass cultivation of Alvengrass—until "Do not stop the economy"

dismissed her, and she was driven from her post. The ministers were keener on tallying a young girl's impudence than her arithmetic of plague. The kingdoms were busier with each other's wars than with the disease. Infected villages burned, orphans overflowed, and the medicine turned into war funds.
People cannot be bound together without an enemy.
Then let there be an enemy—let it be me.

So decided the girl of sixteen, and she crossed the northern mountains. What lived there were not only the sick and the outcast with nowhere to go. The Fanged Folk, the Winged Folk—old races that had killed and been killed by humans for centuries.

The Ashen Haze had crept into their settlements too, and no human doctor ever came. The first human to heal their children, Mia told me, was her. That is why a joke of a story—crowning a human girl as king—came to stand.
The fangs and wings of the Demon Lord's army were real. And because they were real, no one doubted the shroud.

She led them and named herself Demon Lord. The Shrouded Demon Lord. Veil, they say, means "shroud" in the old tongue that survives in the northern mountains. She was born in the north, where that old language still lives. She had declared it from the very beginning: this is a shroud.
It is only that no one ever lifted it.

The kingdoms, panicked by the Demon Lord's advance, stopped their wars, formed an alliance, and redrew the plague cordon as the anti-Demon defense line. Hatred crossed borders faster than any disease, and for the first time in history, humanity became one.
Exactly as she designed.
"There is one thing I don't understand."
I said it. In truth, I think I was beginning to understand. I simply did not want to.
"Why die by my hand at the end? Someone who built all this—why did she need to die? Vanishing would have been enough."
"A Demon Lord who vanishes is a Demon Lord who might return," Mia said. "The alliance could stand on nothing but the Demon Lord's corpse. And—"
There, for the first time, her voice caught.
"She didn't have long. The Ashen Haze."
"There was medicine. Enough to pour into a river."

"The Haze can be cured, if treated early. She caught it in the first years—when Alvengrass was still only a handful. She set the order of treatment by calculation. Children first. Highest odds of recovery first, shortest time left first.

An adult with stamina could stand at the very back of the line—the expanded fields would still be ready in time. That was her arithmetic. Please don't misunderstand. She was not seeking death. She fully intended to be cured herself."
"...It wasn't ready in time?"

"The next year, the royal army burned the fields. War materiel of the Demon Lord's domain, they said. The expansion was delayed, and by then the Haze had taken root in her. Once it takes root, the medicine can only slow it.
Her arithmetic had been correct. What broke it, as ever, was human.
The throne room of the last battle rose up in my mind.

The final day of five years of war. What I saw when I kicked open the doors was no monster of legend. A small figure in a worn cloak, perched shallowly on the throne—about the size of an ordinary person. No horns. No wings. At the time, I paid it no mind.
Whatever shape the Demon Lord wore, killing her was all I had in my head.
That under that cloak was a young woman—only now, from Mia's telling, did I learn it.
The Demon Lord spoke without rising.
"You're late, hero. I nearly died of waiting."
A villain's cheap quip, I thought. I understand now. It was, word for word, a plain statement of fact.
Rising, the Demon Lord spread both arms in a theatrical flourish.
"Come to kill me? Good. That is the one reason to live you have spent twelve years honing. —Use it well."
Mockery, I thought. My eyes burned with hatred. I attacked; the Demon Lord parried—so I wrote in the official history. Demonic swordsmanship, I wrote.

Thinking back, she never once truly crossed blades with me. Mirrors and smoke rigged through the throne room deceived my eyes, contraptions in the floor turned my strikes aside, phantoms threw her voice from elsewhere. Obvious, if I had only thought. An epidemiologist cannot swing a sword.
The fabled sorceries of the Demon Lord, five years of campfire legend, were made of fear, of rumor, and of stagecraft.
It was not a duel. It was a stage. A final battle worthy of legend, and she directed it alone—so that I could go home wearing the face of a hero.
And when the machinery was spent, she stepped out of the smoke and dropped the sword she held.
"End it with this stroke. I won't need a second."
Arrogant nonsense, I wrote. The truth: she no longer had the strength to stay standing for a second.
She laughed as she coughed up blood, I wrote in the official history. A demon's cackle, I wrote.
It was coughing. The Ashen Haze, at its end, brings up blood exactly like that.

She could not be allowed to die of illness. A Demon Lord dead of disease ends no story. Only a Demon Lord slain by a hero completes the legend and makes the alliance eternal. She scheduled even the date of her death to match the final entry of her register.
On the verge of collapse, the Demon Lord said one last thing. This alone I did record in the official history. It was so perfectly the sort of thing a Demon Lord would say.
"Your hatred is my finest work."

For the half year since the subjugation I have chewed on that line as humiliation. Now I chew on it differently. She meant it. The small child she carried out of a burning village had burned hatred for fuel, lived, trained, and reached her throne.
If not her finest work, what would you call me?
"...When my blade went in, her lips moved. I thought she was begging for her life. I didn't listen."
Mia laughed a little, crying.
"That's probably not it."
"Then what did she say?"
"—'Welcome.' It's what she said every time the children came into her kitchen."
The verification was finished, save the oldest entry and the final page—No. 1 and No. 100. Ninety-eight misdeeds had turned inside out into ninety-eight rescues.
I went to No. 1 first. There was nowhere else I could go.
"Misdeed No. 1. Burned the frontier village of Erde. Sixty-one residents, dead. Survivors: one."
Erde. The name of my home.
One survivor. That is me.

My hands shook; for a while I could not touch the documents. After ninety-eight entries I already knew what verification meant. Turn this one over, and my twelve years turn over with it. Pull the foundation from a man built on hatred, and what remains?
Still, I investigated. This verification began as a way to hate her. Seeing it through to the end was the least I owed—to whom, I no longer knew.
I went to Erde. For the first time in twelve years.

The village was nowhere. The outlines of house foundations sunk in grass; only the well's rim left standing, white as teeth. Wind. The smell of grass. Birds, far off. The place I was born was made of sounds.

At the edge of the site stood small cairns of stacked stone. Sixty-one—I knew without counting. No name of the builder anywhere. Only, beneath the largest stone, unnumbered markers set with her dutiful care, each facing the same way.
Work that appears in no register of misdeeds—she had done it here.
In the war office's archive of old documents, an order surfaced.
"Re: Purification of Erde Village." Site of Ashen Haze outbreak; to be incinerated, residents included.
The scheduled date of execution—the day after the Demon Lord's raid.
The army had meant to come. Had meant to burn the villagers with the village. The Demon Lord arrived exactly one day ahead of them.
Erde was the first village where the Ashen Haze broke out.
In the margin of Entry One, in that hand, it says:
"Of sixty-one, fifty-eight rescued. Three beyond saving. Of these, one woman, lucid to the end. Entrusted me with her child."
My mother did not die by fire.

It was the disease. When the Demon Lord came, she was already beyond help. And with her last strength, she entrusted the fever-stricken child at her side to the "Demon Lord" who had come to burn the village.

Fever-stricken—so that is why that night survives only as fire and a cloak. High fever is the first symptom of the Ashen Haze. At six years old, I had already caught it. And yet here I am, alive. Mia's words found me late, and went in deep.
Her medicine always went to the children first.

I think of the sixty-one cairns at Erde. Only three of them hold anyone at all. The other fifty-eight are empty graves for people who live on today under other names. The shroud extended, dutifully, even over a graveyard.
And still she built all fifty-eight empty graves with the same care as the true ones.
I took the name tag from my chest.

The tag once tied to my collar, the first thing that was ever mine. In the common tongue, "Ash" means cinders. A child picked out of a burn site, so they named him for ashes—so I had always believed. The first word of my hatred. I never knew who named me.
I set the tag beside the ledger.
That tidy, oddly dutiful hand, slanting up to the right.
The same hand.
The same hand wrote them both.

And my first memory came back with the sheath off. Fire. Smoke. The stiffness of a black cloak running with me in its arms. For twelve years I had dreamed it over and over as the nightmare of being taken. It was the memory of being carried out. That night, I was in her arms.
The marginal note continued.

"The child's name is by his mother's last will. 'Give this child a reason to live.' The name is Ash. In the old tongue of her homeland, it means dawn. It sounds the same as 'ash' in the common tongue. When I noticed that, I decided to use the coincidence.
I hope he misreads it as the name of cinders. Hatred makes a reason to live. It keeps longer than hunger, longer than despair. This child will hate me, and survive."
Ash.
Dawn.
Two words in a single sound. Read in the common tongue, Ash is what remains after burning. Read in his mother's old northern tongue, the same sound names the hour when night turns to light.
For twelve years the world read my name as cinders. I introduced myself as cinders. Every time I swore revenge, I touched this tag.
But my mother had called me dawn from the very beginning.
My mother, too, was northern-born, they say. That is why she—only she, born to the same old language—could hear a dying woman's last word, alone in all the world, and hear it right.
What I gripped as proof of hatred had been, from the start, a prayer made by two people. Inside one name, my mother's wish and her design stood back to back for twelve years.
The final page of the register. Dated the morning of the last battle.
Having verified ninety-nine entries through No. 1, I already knew: among the ninety-nine "misdeeds," not one person had died by her hand. Surely No. 100 would turn over just the same.
On the last page, it said:
"Misdeed No. 100.
From one child, I stole the truth of his mother's death.
I gave him hatred. I closed his hand around a sword.
I spent his twelve years for the ending of my story.
Entries One through Ninety-nine are apparatus.
Entry One Hundred alone is sin.
This alone is true."
That night, in the Demon Lord's study, I wept aloud for the first time in my life.
The woman who wore ninety-nine infamies without moving an eyebrow. The woman who bound the world's hatred like a ledger of accounts and carried it alone.
Only what she did to me, she called sin.

That she stayed by my dying mother; that she gave me a name; that she gave me a reason to live; that she took even the role of dying by my hand—she bundled all of it into a single sin, counted it once, and died.
No apology. No defense. One line.
This alone is true.
That meticulous, right-slanting hand ends there. Every page after is white.
I do not remember what hour I stopped crying. I changed the candle, turned the register back to its first page, and this time read it as a book of accounts.
I summed the "dead" of all hundred entries.
The dead of the burned villages. The dead of the poisoned river. The stolen children. The total of victims dutifully recorded in the register: four thousand eight hundred sixteen.
I set it against my verification. Those living under changed names, those who wintered downstream of the medicine river, the orphans raised in the valley. I counted every one that could be counted.
Four thousand eight hundred thirteen.
Three short.
I did not need to recount to know which three. Erde village. "Three beyond saving." My mother among them.

For twelve years she recorded the number of people she saved disguised as the number she killed—and within it, only the three she failed to reach were entered as true dead. The most hated criminal record in the world was the world's most accurate ledger of lives saved.
The three lines that never balanced were her only regret.
I wept once more, and then put the compiler's face back on. There was work left. The work of finishing hers.
What I wrote in the official history, you already know.
The Demon Lord Veil ravaged the continent with a hundred misdeeds, and the hero Ash struck her down. And so the world was saved.

I considered writing the truth. Many times. But truth would split the alliance. The moment the Demon Lord was known to be good, the kingdoms would look at one another and ask: then who is the next enemy? The two hundred fourteen living under new names, and the three hundred children, would be hunted as the Demon Lord's
accomplices.

And yet, if the valley stands untouched to this day, it is not thanks to my mercy. By rights the victors' armies should have poured in and burned it under the name of hunting remnants. But no one can enter. The soldiers stop at the valley's mouth, afraid of the curse.

That last proclamation without a deadline—"Whosoever touches my land and my people after my death shall bear a curse unto the last generation." A general who scoffs at curses still cannot march soldiers who fear one. The woman who set a deadline on every other decree left the deadline off that one page alone.

Because it was not a warning to flee. It was written as a fence, to stand forever. Twelve years of carefully stacked infamy, converted whole into a shield for the people she left behind. Even the hatred that would outlive her, she gave a use.
So the truth is all the more unwritable. Reveal the trick of the curse, and the fence disappears. A curse with its secret out protects no one.

And sometimes I think. The shelf with no lock. The numbers that can be checked against the registries. That ledger was not hidden. It was written to be read—by the one person with the right to write history.
Only the testimony of the hero who killed her could complete her false villainy.
So I wrote it. The biography of the most hated woman in the world, written by the one man who knows the truth. I lined up nothing but facts, and lied.
If the register of misdeeds needs a No. 101, it is me.

This year again, in some square somewhere, they will burn the Demon Lord in effigy. Children will kick up the ash, laughing. I no longer try to stop the festival. As long as hatred gathers on a single doll, it does not turn toward one's neighbors.
She would have called it disease control.

Mia now runs a clinic in the valley that was the Demon Lord's land. When a child comes in she says "Welcome"—a habit I doubt she notices. And the valley's children still grow up rehearsing insults for a dead Demon Lord. Her stinginess. Her meanness. Her heartlessness.
The kindest insults in the world are still a dialect spoken only inside that valley.

As for me, I still wear the name tag. The habit of touching it has not healed either. Only its meaning has changed. The gesture that once confirmed my revenge is now the gesture of being called—by the two of them.
Dawn, they say.
Now, then.

This forbidden book will be sealed, not to be opened until a hundred years after my death. Who you are, reading it now, I have no way to know. A historian; a king; or only someone who wandered into the archive.
But one thing is certain.
When you read the legend in the preface, you read her exactly so: the Demon Lord who burned villages, poisoned a river, stole children—an evil that deserved the sword.
There is no shame in it. The whole world read her that way. I read her that way for twelve years. She designed every word to be read that way.

And now you cannot hate her. Not because you were saved, like the valley folk. Not because she gave you a name, like me. Only because you know. You are the first person to stand on her side having received nothing at all.

Welcome to this side. The truth is a narrow place, but it is not empty. The valley's children are here, and Mia, and I. And from today, you. That the dark is deepest just before dawn is, according to her ledger, merely an observed fact.
Let me quote, one last time, the closing line of the official history. This time, you will read it right.
—And so the world was saved.
It was the ending exactly as she wrote it.
May a good dawn find you.
( Fin )
